title: Review: Communicable diseases
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank, except where marked for AQA GCSE Biology (8461) (status of the source: authored-gated-unreviewed). Terms and clues: 4.3.1-c03 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.3.1-c05 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.3.1-c25 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.3.1-c20 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition. Questions: 4.3.1-q01, 4.3.1-q05, 4.3.1-q02, 4.3.1-q03, 4.3.1-q07, 4.3.1-q10, 4.3.1-q11, 4.3.1-q16, 4.3.1-q04, 4.3.1-q06, 4.3.1-q09, 4.3.1-q13. The matching task revisits terms from the worlds it reviews, in a new mix. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: toxin
items.clue: A poison that bacteria may produce.

items.label: measles
items.clue: A viral disease showing symptoms of fever and a red skin rash.

items.label: clinical trial
items.clue: The stage of drug development that uses healthy volunteers and patients.

items.label: antibiotic
items.clue: A medicine, such as penicillin, that helps to cure bacterial disease by killing infective bacteria inside the body.

options.text: A bacterium that causes an infectious disease
A poison that damages tissues and makes us ill
A microorganism that lives inside the body cells
A microorganism that causes infectious disease

questions.explanation: Pathogens are microorganisms that cause infectious disease. They may be viruses, bacteria, protists or fungi, and may infect plants or animals.

questions.stem: How is the spread of salmonella food poisoning controlled in the UK?

options.text: People are vaccinated against salmonella
Poultry are vaccinated against salmonella
Poultry are treated with strong antibiotics
People are given painkillers to cure it

questions.explanation: Salmonella food poisoning is spread by bacteria ingested in food, and in the UK poultry are vaccinated against salmonella to control the spread.

questions.stem: Purple and black spots have appeared on the leaves of a rose bush in a garden. How is this disease most likely to reach the other rose bushes in the garden?

options.text: By insects moving between the plants
By direct contact between the leaves
By toxins spreading through the soil
By water or wind in the environment

questions.explanation: Rose black spot is a fungal disease that is spread in the environment by water or wind, so it can cross the gap between plants that never touch.

questions.stem: What kind of pathogen causes malaria?

options.text: A protist spread to humans by mosquitos
A bacterium spread to humans by mosquitos
A mosquito that bites and infects humans
A virus that reproduces in human cells

questions.explanation: The pathogens that cause malaria are protists, and the malarial protist has a life cycle that includes the mosquito.

questions.stem: Bacteria in the blood are releasing toxins. Which action of the white blood cells deals with those toxins?

options.text: The production of antibodies
The engulfing of the bacteria
The production of antitoxins
The production of stomach acid

questions.explanation: White blood cells help to defend against pathogens by antitoxin production, and antitoxins counteract the toxins that bacteria produce.

questions.stem: A large proportion of the population in a town is vaccinated against measles. What is the effect on the people in that town who are not vaccinated?

options.text: They are equally likely to catch measles
They are made immune to measles as well
They are less likely to catch measles
They must be given antibiotics instead

questions.explanation: The spread of pathogens can be reduced by immunising a large proportion of the population, so an unvaccinated person is less likely to meet the measles virus.

questions.stem: A patient has a viral infection and a painful sore throat. Which treatment is appropriate, and why?

options.text: Antibiotics, which kill the pathogen
Painkillers, which destroy the virus
Painkillers, which treat the symptoms
Antitoxins, which kill the pathogen

questions.explanation: Painkillers and other medicines are used to treat the symptoms of disease but do not kill pathogens, so they are the appropriate treatment for the pain of a viral infection.

questions.stem: Which drug is correctly matched with the source it originally came from?

options.text: Aspirin is extracted from foxgloves
Penicillin is extracted from foxgloves
Digitalis is extracted from foxgloves
Digitalis is extracted from the willow

questions.explanation: Traditionally drugs were extracted from plants and microorganisms, and the heart drug digitalis originates from foxgloves.

questions.stem: A health agency wants to reduce the number of malaria cases in a region. Which approach should it use?

options.text: Treating infected people with antibiotics
Stopping mosquitos breeding and using nets
Vaccinating whole populations against it
Avoiding direct contact with infected people

questions.explanation: The spread of malaria is controlled by preventing the vectors, mosquitos, from breeding and by using mosquito nets to avoid being bitten.

questions.stem: Which of these is a non-specific defence system of the human body?

options.text: The nose produces antibodies to attack pathogens
The stomach produces acid that kills pathogens
Cilia in the trachea destroy trapped pathogens
White blood cells in the skin trap pathogens

questions.explanation: The stomach is one of the non-specific defence systems of the human body: it produces hydrochloric acid that kills pathogens in swallowed food and mucus.

questions.stem: What is introduced into the body during a vaccination?

options.text: Dead or inactive forms of a pathogen
Ready-made antibodies from donors
Live and active forms of a pathogen
An antibiotic that kills pathogens

questions.explanation: Vaccination involves introducing small quantities of dead or inactive forms of a pathogen into the body to stimulate the white blood cells to produce antibodies.

questions.stem: Why is it difficult to develop drugs that kill viruses?

options.text: Viruses live in cells, so tissues are damaged
Viruses reproduce outside the body's cells
Viruses make toxins that destroy the drugs
Viruses are easily destroyed by antibiotics

questions.explanation: Viruses live and reproduce inside cells, so it is difficult to develop drugs that kill viruses without also damaging the body's tissues.
